content.content:
# Hub Rate limits

To protect our platform's integrity and ensure availability to as many AI community members as possible, we enforce rate limits on all requests made to the Hugging Face Hub.

We define different rate limits for distinct classes of requests. We distinguish three main buckets:

- **Hub APIs**
  - e.g. model or dataset search, repo creation, user management, etc. All endpoints that belong to this bucket are documented in [Hub API Endpoints](./api).
- **Resolvers**
  - They're all the URLs that contain a `/resolve/` segment in their path, which serve user-generated content from the Hub. Concretely, those are the URLs that are constructed by open source libraries (transformers, datasets, vLLM, llama.cpp, …) or AI applications (LM Studio, Jan, ollama, …) to download model/dataset files from HF.
  - Specifically, this is the ["Resolve a file" endpoint](https://huggingface-openapi.hf.space/#tag/models/get/apiresolve-cachemodelsnamespacereporevpath) documented in our OpenAPI spec.
  - Resolve requests are heavily used by the community, and since we optimize our infrastructure to serve them with maximum efficiency, the rate limits for Resolvers are the highest.
- **Pages**
  - All the Web pages we host on huggingface.co.
  - Usually Web browsing requests are made by humans, hence rate limits don't need to be as high as the above mentioned programmatic endpoints.

> [!TIP]
> All values are defined over 5-minute windows, which allows for some level of "burstiness" from an application or developer's point of view.

If you, your organization, or your application need higher rate limits, we encourage you to upgrade your account to PRO, Team, or Enterprise. We prioritize support requests from PRO, Team, and Enterprise customers – see built-in limits in [Rate limit Tiers](#rate-limit-tiers).

## Billing dashboard

At any point, you can check your rate limit status on your (or your org’s) Billing page: https://huggingface.co/settings/billing

![dashboard for rate limits](https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/5dd96eb166059660ed1ee413/0pzQQyuVG3c9tWjCqrX9Y.png)

On the right side, you will see three gauges, one for each bucket of Requests.

Each bucket presents the number of current (last 5 minutes) requests, and the number of allowed requests based on your user account or organization plan.

Whenever you exceed the limit in the past 5 minutes (the view is updated in real-time), the bar will turn red.

Note: You can use the context switcher to easily switch between your user account and your orgs.

## HTTP Headers

Whenever you or your organization hits a rate limit, you will receive a **429** `Too Many Requests` HTTP error.

We implement the mechanism described in the [IETF draft (Version 9)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers/) titled “RateLimit HTTP header fields for HTTP” (also known as `draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers`).

The goal is to define standardized HTTP headers that servers can use to advertise quota / rate-limit policies and communicate current usage / limits to clients so that they can avoid being throttled.

Precisely, we implement the following headers:

| Header                 | Purpose / Meaning                                                                                                                       |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **`RateLimit`**        | The total allowed rate limit for the current window. “How many requests (of this type) you’re allowed to perform.”                      |
| **`RateLimit-Policy`** | Carries the rate limit policy itself (e.g. “100 requests per 5 minutes”). It’s informative; shows what policy the client is subject to. |

A set of examples is as follows:

| Header                 | Example                                                                                               |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **`RateLimit`**        | `"api\|pages\|resolvers";r=[remaining];t=[seconds remaining until reset]`                             |
| **`RateLimit-Policy`** | `"fixed window";"api\|\pages\|resolvers";q=[total allowed for window];w=[window duration in seconds]` |

## Rate limit Tiers

Here are the current rate limits (in September '25) based on your plan:

| Plan                                                                      | API      | Resolvers | Pages  |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | --------- | ------ |
| Anonymous user (per IP address)                                           | 500 \*   | 3,000 \*  | 100 \* |
| Free user                                                                 | 1,000 \* | 5,000 \*  | 200 \* |
| PRO user                                                                  | 2,500    | 12,000    | 400    |
| Team organization                                                         | 3,000    | 20,000    | 400    |
| Enterprise organization                                                   | 6,000    | 50,000    | 600    |
| Enterprise Plus organization                                              | 10,000   | 100,000   | 1,000  |
| Enterprise Plus organization  With "Higher Hub Rate Limits" enabled   | 100,000  | 500,000   | 10,000 |
| Academia Hub organization                                                 | 3,000    | 20,000    | 400    |

\* Anonymous and Free users are subject to change over time depending on platform health 🤞

> [!NOTE]
> All quotas are calculated over 5-minute fixed windows.

Note: For organizations, rate limits are applied individually to each member, not shared among members.

## What if I get rate-limited

First, make sure you always pass a `HF_TOKEN`, and it is passed downstream to all libraries or applications that download _stuff_ from the Hub.

This is the number one reason users get rate limited and is a very easy fix.

Despite passing `HF_TOKEN` if you are still rate limited, you can:

- spread out your requests over longer periods of time
- replace Hub API calls with Resolver calls, whenever possible (Resolver rate limits are much higher and much more optimized).
- upgrade to PRO, Team, or Enterprise.

## Smart rate limit handling with `huggingface_hub`

The Hub Python Library [`huggingface_hub`](https://huggingface.co/docs/huggingface_hub/index) (version **1.2.0+**) includes smart retry handling for rate limit errors.

When a 429 error occurs, the SDK automatically parses the `RateLimit` header to extract the exact number of seconds until the rate limit resets, then waits precisely that duration before retrying. This applies to file downloads (i.e. Resolvers) and paginated Hub API calls (list models, datasets, spaces, etc.).

**We strongly recommend using `huggingface_hub` for all programmatic access to the Hub** to benefit from this optimized retry behavior and avoid implementing custom rate limit handling.

## Granular user action Rate limits

In addition to those main classes of rate limits, we enforce limits on certain specific kinds of user actions, like:

- repo creation
- repo commits
- discussions and comments
- moderation actions
- etc.

We don't currently document the rate limits for those specific actions, given they tend to change over time more often. If you get quota errors, we encourage you to upgrade your account to PRO, Team, or Enterprise.
Feel free to get in touch with us via the support team.

# Spec Kit Analysis

**License:** MIT open source license

**Latest Release:** v1.0.0 (released one year after initial commit; exact date not specified in content)

**Core Slash Commands:**
- `/speckit.constitution` – Project principles

- `/speckit.plan` – Technical implementation plans
- `/speckit.tasks` – Actionable task lists
- `/speckit.implement` – Execute tasks

- `/speckit.clarify` – Clarify underspecified areas

**External Search Capability:** The content does not indicate Spec Kit performs external code or repository searching. The toolkit focuses on structured development workflows within a user's own project directory.

The command-line interface supports basic directory analysis and GitHub repository processing:
```bash
gitingest /path/to/directory
gitingest https://github.com/user/repo
```
Additional flags enable private repo access via `--token`, submodule inclusion, and customizable output formats.

**Python API:**
Both synchronous and asynchronous functions are available:
```python
from gitingest import ingest
summary, tree, content = ingest("path/to/directory")
```
The library supports environment variables for GitHub tokens and works in Jupyter notebooks.

- File structure and size statistics
- Token count estimation (via tiktoken)
- Private repository support with GitHub PAT
- Respects `.gitignore` by default
- Browser extensions for Chrome and Firefox

**Hosted Service:** gitingest.com provides free web access without installation.

**Technology Stack:** Built with FastAPI (backend), Tailwind CSS (frontend), and integrates Sentry for error tracking.

# SWE-bench Multimodal: RAG Baselines and Performance

## RAG Setup
The authors adapted retrieval-augmented generation from prior work: "We adapt the prompt template used in Jimenez et al. (2024a) to use a JavaScript example for patch generation instead of Python."

RAG systems significantly underperformed interactive agent approaches. The results showed:

The paper notes that visual problem-solving capability was critical. ## ContextBench Overview

ContextBench is a process-oriented evaluation of context retrieval in coding agents. It consists of 1,136 issue-resolution tasks from 66 repositories across eight programming languages, each augmented with human-annotated gold contexts.

## Methodology

The benchmark implements an automated evaluation framework that tracks agent trajectories and measures context recall, precision, and efficiency throughout issue resolution. By providing verified gold contexts and automated retrieval metrics, ContextBench facilitates transparent, reproducible, and fine-grained assessment of how coding agents interact with large-scale codebases.

## Key Findings

Using ContextBench, the researchers evaluated four frontier LLMs and five coding agents, finding that sophisticated agent scaffolding yields only marginal gains in context retrieval, LLMs consistently favor recall over precision, and substantial gaps exist between explored and utilized information.

## Publication Details

The paper was authored by Han Li, Letian Zhu, Bohan Zhang, Rili Feng, Jiaming Wang, Yue Pan, Earl T. Barr, Federica Sarro, Zhaoyang Chu, and He Ye in 2026, published as arXiv:2602.05892.

## SBOM Format Requirements

The CRA does not mandate a specific format, and as of today there are no final harmonised EN standards nor delegated acts on the format: in practice teams adopt CycloneDX or SPDX. CycloneDX was created by the OWASP Foundation and is compact and strong on security and vulnerability use cases, while SPDX originated at the Linux Foundation and is standardised as ISO/IEC 5962, strong on detailed licence metadata.

## 2026 Commission Implementing Regulations

The European Commission implementing rules (in progress in 2026) are converging on CycloneDX JSON for standardization. More specifically, Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) in CycloneDX 1.5 or SPDX 2.3 is mandatory, generated on every build according to the European Commission Implementing Regulation draft.

## Timeline and Key Dates

The bulk of the regulation (essential requirements, manufacturer obligations and technical documentation) applies from 11 December 2027. However, notifications will go through the CRA Single Reporting Platform operated by ENISA, which will be operational by September 2026.

## SBOM Requirements

Annex I, Part II, point 1 requires documenting the product's components in a software bill of materials in a commonly used, machine-readable format, covering at least the top-level dependencies.

# CRA Treatment of Free and Open-Source Software

## When FOSS Is Out of Scope

Non-commercial FOSS is excluded from CRA requirements. Specifically, "the provision of products with digital elements qualifying as free and open-source software that are not monetised by their manufacturers should not be considered to be a commercial activity." Additionally, individual code contributors are exempt—the CRA "does not apply to developers who contribute with source code to free and open-source software that are not under their responsibility."

## Open-Source Software Stewards

The CRA introduces a novel regulatory category for entities providing sustained support to FOSS projects intended for commercial use. These stewards are legal persons who "provide support on a sustained basis for the development of such products...and play a main role in ensuring their viability."

## Steward Obligations

Open-source software stewards face lighter regulatory requirements than manufacturers. They must establish "a cybersecurity policy to foster secure development and handling of vulnerabilities," cooperate with market surveillance authorities, and report actively exploited vulnerabilities. Notably, stewards are exempt from administrative fines under Article 64(10).

## Integration of FOSS into Commercial Products

The document does not address security attestation requirements or specific obligations when integrating FOSS components into commercial products. When manufacturers place commercial products containing FOSS on the market, they face standard manufacturer obligations, but specific integration requirements are not detailed in this resource.

The connector indexes **Pull Requests and Issues** from specified repositories:

# Search

You can easily search anything on the Hub with **Full-text search**. We index model cards, dataset cards, and Spaces app.py files.

Go directly to https://huggingface.co/search or, using the search bar at the top of https://huggingface.co, you can select "Try Full-text search" to help find what you seek on the Hub across models, datasets, and Spaces:

## Filter with ease

By default, models, datasets, & spaces are being searched when a user enters a query. If one prefers, one can filter to search only models, datasets, or spaces.

Moreover, one can copy & share the URL from one's browser's address bar, which should contain the filter information as URL query. For example, when one searches for a query `llama` with a filter to show `Spaces` only, one gets URL https://huggingface.co/search/full-text?q=llama&type=space

# Repomix MCP Tools and Features

## Available MCP Tools

Repomix exposes six primary tools when running as an MCP server:

1. **pack_codebase** - Packages local directories into consolidated XML files for AI analysis, including codebase metrics and formatted code content.

2. **pack_remote_repository** - "Fetches, clones, and packages a GitHub repository into a consolidated XML file for AI analysis."

3. **read_repomix_output** - Retrieves previously generated output files with optional line range specification for partial reading.

4. **grep_repomix_output** - Searches Repomix outputs using regex patterns with configurable context lines before/after matches.

5. **file_system_read_file** - Reads file contents relative to workspace root (sandbox mode only).

6. **file_system_read_directory** - Lists directory contents with file/directory indicators (sandbox mode only).

## Key Features

**Compression Mode**: Tree-sitter compression extracts code signatures while removing implementation details, reducing token usage by approximately 70% while maintaining semantic meaning.

**Remote Repository Support**: The `pack_remote_repository` tool accepts GitHub URLs or `user/repo` format, enabling analysis of external codebases.

**Sandbox Mode**: The `--sandbox` flag confines file tools to a specified workspace directory, restricting path access to prevent security risks when exposing the server to untrusted clients.

**Output Patterns**: Per-file configuration allows selective compression or directory-structure-only modes for different file types, providing granular control over processing.

# Paper Summary: CoREB Benchmark

**Title:** "Beyond Retrieval: A Multitask Benchmark and Model for Code Search"

**Authors:** Siqiao Xue, Zihan Liao, Jin Qin, Ziyin Zhang, Yixiang Mu, Fan Zhou, Hang Yu

**Date:** Submitted May 6, 2026; revised May 8, 2026

## Benchmark Contents

**CoREB** (code retrieval and reranking benchmark) encompasses:
- **Tasks:** Three evaluation scenarios—text-to-code, code-to-text, and code-to-code searches
- **Languages:** Five programming languages
- **Source:** Built from counterfactually rewritten LiveCodeBench problems with graded relevance judgments
- **Scope:** Covers the full code search pipeline beyond first-stage retrieval

## Models Evaluated

The study benchmarked "eleven embedding models and five rerankers" across the three task types.

## Key Findings

The authors report that specialized embeddings achieve roughly 2× performance gains on code-to-code tasks, yet no single model excels across all three tasks. Short keyword queries (mimicking real developer behavior) caused dramatic performance degradation. Their fine-tuned CoREB-Reranker became "the first to achieve consistent gains across all three tasks."

## Relation to Prior Work

The paper references LiveCodeBench as source material but does not explicitly discuss CodeSearchNet or CoIR within the provided abstract.

# Critique of Vendor-Run Code Review Benchmarks

## Dataset Sizes

The article identifies a critical weakness: **"50 PRs across 5 repos is a small dataset"** (Greptile). The author argues that statistical noise becomes problematic at this scale, noting that **"with 50 data points, a handful of edge cases can swing aggregate results significantly."** The piece recommends treating anything under 100 entries with skepticism.

## Self-Reported vs. Independent Re-Evaluation

The most damning example involves Greptile's benchmark. The vendor reported **"82% recall, with a 24-point gap over the next best tool."** However, when Augment Code independently evaluated the same five repositories, Greptile's score dropped dramatically to **"45%, not 82%."** The author emphasizes: **"Same repos, wildly different results depending on who runs the benchmark."**

## Methodological Issues

The article identifies several structural problems:

- **Ground truth reliability**: Qodo's benchmark used **"bugs an LLM invented and inserted,"** creating questionable validity since **"The ground truth is LLM-generated, the evaluation uses LLM-as-a-judge."**

- **Lack of transparency**: Qodo's actual ground truth wasn't published, meaning **"nobody can reproduce the scoring."**

- **Self-evaluation bias**: The author notes that **"Designers naturally understand their own criteria and optimize for them, consciously or not,"** and observes that **"every vendor that has published one wins their own"** benchmark (as of February 2026).

# Deep Search: Overview

## What It Does
Deep Search is an agentic code search tool that "understands natural language questions about your codebase" and "returns a detailed answer." Users can continue conversations with follow-up questions to explore relevant code further.

## How It Works
The tool operates through an agentic loop where the AI agent "intelligently use[s] tools to explore the codebase," gradually refining understanding across iterations until confident in its answer. It leverages Sourcegraph's Code Search and Code Navigation features, with "all processing happens within your Sourcegraph instance."

The documentation mentions the agent can run "small Lua scripts for analysis" within a sandboxed environment that has "no network, system, or general filesystem access" and only access to Sourcegraph-provided modules for searching, file reading, and formatting.

## Plan Availability
The documentation does not specify which pricing tiers include Deep Search. It notes the tool is "only available to customers using the Sourcegraph Model Provider" and is unavailable to those using bring-your-own-key (BYOK) model configurations.

## API & MCP Support
Deep Search integrates with "Sourcegraph APIs" and the "MCP server." An experimental Deep Search API exists with a migration guide available.

## Limits & Credits
Deep Search "consumes credits from your Sourcegraph subscription's credit balance." Administrators can set entitlements (e.g., "60 Deep Search per hour") and enforce role-based access control to manage usage.

## Quality Claims
Each response includes "a detailed list of sources" showing exactly which searches and files contributed to answers, supporting transparency and further exploration.

# Sourcegraph MCP Server Summary

## Tools Available
The MCP server provides these primary tools:

**File & Repository Operations:** `read_file` (retrieve file contents), `list_files` (directory browsing), `list_repos` (repository discovery)

**Code Search:** `keyword_search` (exact matching), `nls_search` (semantic search), `evaluator` (Lua-based aggregation)

**Code Navigation:** `go_to_definition`, `find_references`

**Version Control:** `commit_search`, `diff_search`, `compare_revisions`, `get_contributor_repos`

**Specialized Tools:** `code_finder` (fast agentic search), `deepsearch` (complex codebase analysis)

## Endpoint Pattern
The service uses this URL structure: `https://your-sourcegraph-instance.com/.api/mcp` with variants:
- `/.api/mcp` (core tools)
- `/.api/mcp/all` (full suite)
- `/.api/mcp/deepsearch` (Deep Search only)

## Authentication
The server supports "OAuth 2.0 through Dynamic Client Registration or pre-registered OAuth clients, as well as Sourcegraph access tokens." Users need the `MCP#ACCESS` permission.

## Plan Information
The documentation doesn't specify pricing tiers or plan eligibility. Code Finder usage is "metered against your instance's entitlement," suggesting quota-based access rather than plan-based restrictions.

# EU Product Liability Directive 2024/2853 - Key Scope Provisions

## Software Coverage
The directive explicitly includes software as a product. Article 4(1) defines product as "all movables, even if integrated into, or inter-connected with, another movable or an immovable; it includes electricity, digital manufacturing files, raw materials and **software**."

## Free and Open-Source Software Exemption
Article 2(2) provides a critical exemption: "This Directive does not apply to free and open-source software that is developed or supplied outside the course of a commercial activity."

This means FOSS projects developed non-commercially remain outside the directive's scope, protecting volunteer developers and research initiatives from liability.

## Application Timeline
The directive establishes a transition period. Article 2(1) specifies: "This Directive shall apply to products placed on the market or put into service after 9 December 2026."

Article 22 requires member states to implement the directive by the same deadline, with Article 21 confirming the previous directive (85/374/EEC) continues applying to products placed on the market before December 9, 2026.

# Copilot Repository Indexing for Semantic Code Search

## What Gets Indexed
Copilot automatically indexes repositories to enable semantic code search—a meaning-based search approach that goes beyond exact text matching. The system indexes "the semantic code search index for the repository" to improve context-enriched responses about code structure and logic.

## Automatic Indexing Process
Indexing operates automatically in the background. "Initial indexing can take up to 60 seconds for a large repository." After the first index is created, subsequent updates happen much faster—"the index will typically be automatically updated to include the latest changes within seconds of you starting a new conversation."

Manual configuration is not required for GitHub repositories, though non-GitHub repositories require administrators to enable the semantic indexing policy.

## Repository Limits
There are no constraints on repository quantity: "There is no limit to how many repositories you can index." The documentation does not specify size limitations.

## Index Usage
Once created, indexes serve multiple Copilot components:
- **Copilot Chat** in GitHub and Visual Studio Code uses indexes to answer questions about repository code
- **Copilot cloud agent** leverages semantic code search "to find relevant code based on meaning, rather than relying solely on exact text matches"

The indexed data supports informed, context-aware responses without training model improvements on user repositories.

# Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 Key Provisions Summary

## Application Dates

**Article 71** establishes a phased implementation schedule:
- General application: "11 December 2027"
- Chapter IV (conformity assessment): "11 September 2026"
- Article 14 (important products): "11 June 2026"

## Software Bill of Materials Requirement

**Annex I, Part II, point (1)** mandates that manufacturers must provide documentation identifying "top-level dependencies" in a format that "enables automated tools to process such information."

## Third-Party Component Due Diligence

**Article 13(5)** requires manufacturers integrating external components—including open-source software not commercially distributed—to perform due diligence through actions such as: verifying components have received "regular security updates," checking against vulnerability databases, or conducting "additional security tests."

## Open-Source Software Steward Obligations

**Article 24** establishes that entities providing sustained development support for free and open-source software intended for commercial use must: establish vulnerability disclosure policies, maintain a single contact point for users, and handle vulnerability notifications—but are prohibited from affixing CE marking to such products.

# Blackbird Code Search Architecture Facts

**Ngram Strategy:**
"sparse grams" approach with dynamic gram sizes instead of fixed trigrams. The system "use[s] the exact same algorithm" at query time to "keep only the covering ngrams, as the others are redundant."

**Scale:**
- "45 million repositories" currently searchable
- "15.5 billion documents"
- "115 TB of code" indexed

**Index Efficiency:**
- Original content: 115 TB
- After deduplication and delta indexing: "around 28 TB of unique content"
- Final index size: "just 25 TB, which includes not only all the indices (including the ngrams), but also a compressed copy of all unique content"

**Performance:**
- Ingest capacity: "around 120,000 documents per second"
- Full corpus re-index time: "about 18 hours"
- Per-shard p99 latency: "on the order of 100 ms"
- Upper bound throughput: "something like 640 queries per second"

**Deduplication:**
Built on "Git's use of content addressable hashing" by sharding "by Git blob object ID" to avoid duplication while distributing load evenly.

**Ranking:**
Documents ranked by relevance with "lazy iterators" returning "sorted document IDs (the IDs are assigned based on the ranking of each document)."

# Hugging Face MCP Server

The Hugging Face MCP (Model Context Protocol) Server connects your MCP‑compatible AI assistant (for example Codex, Cursor, VS Code extensions, Zed, ChatGPT or Claude Desktop) directly to the Hugging Face Hub. Once connected, your assistant can search and explore Hub resources and use community tools, all from within your editor, chat or CLI.

## What you can do

- Search and explore Hub resources: models, datasets, Spaces, papers and more.
- Search the Hugging Face documentation with natural language queries.
- Schedule and run Jobs and use sandboxes
- Run community tools via MCP‑compatible Gradio apps hosted on [Spaces](https://hf.co/spaces).
- Bring results back into your assistant with metadata, links, and context.

## Get started

1. Open your [MCP settings](https://huggingface.co/settings/mcp) while logged in.

2. Pick your client: select your MCP‑compatible client (for example Cursor, VS Code, Zed, Claude Desktop). The page shows client‑specific instructions and a ready‑to‑copy configuration snippet.

3. Paste and restart: copy the snippet into your client’s MCP configuration, save, and restart/reload the client. You should see “Hugging Face” (or similar) listed as a connected MCP server in your client.

> [!TIP]
> The settings page generates the exact configuration your client expects. Use it rather than writing config by hand.

![MCP Settings Example](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/hf-mcp-settings-new.png)

## Using the server

After connecting, ask your assistant to use the Hugging Face tools. Example prompts:

- “Search Hugging Face models for Qwen 3.6 Quantizations.”
- “Find a Space that can transcribe audio files.”
- “Show datasets about weather time‑series.”
- “Create a 1024 x 1024 image of a cat ghibli style.”
- "How do I use LoRA adapters with PEFT?" (uses Documentation Semantic Search)
- "Find papers about vision-language models."

Your assistant will navigate the Hub using  tools exposed by the MCP Server (including Spaces you have selected, as shown in the next section) and return results (titles, owners, downloads, links, and so on). You can then open the resource on the Hub or continue iterating in the same chat.

![HF MCP with Spaces in VS Code](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/hf-mcp-vscode.png)

## Built-in Tools

Most Hub tasks can be efficiently completed with the built in `hf_fs` tool. It lets your assistant efficiently navigate the Hub, including semantic searches of Documents and Spaces.

You can configure extra tools from your [MCP settings](https://huggingface.co/settings/mcp) page.

| Tool | Description |
|------|-------------|

# GitHub License Detection Overview

## Detection Method

GitHub uses **Licensee**, an open source Ruby Gem, to identify project licenses. The system matches a project's `LICENSE` file contents "against a short list of known licenses." This approach focuses solely on the LICENSE file itself, not dependencies or documentation references.

## License Object Fields

The API returns standardized license information with these key fields:

- **`key`**: Unique identifier for the license
- **`name`**: Human-readable license name
- **`spdx_id`**: Identifier conforming to the SPDX specification
- **`url`**: Reference URL for the license

Additional fields in detailed responses include `description`, `permissions`, `conditions`, and `limitations`.

## Behavior When Detection Fails

The documentation does not explicitly describe a "NOASSERTION" fallback or other specific behavior when license detection fails. However, the response schema shows the `license` field can be **`null`**, indicating no license was successfully matched.

The API handles missing licenses by returning `null` rather than providing a default assertion value, allowing consumers to distinguish between detected and undetected licenses.

# OSS Review Toolkit (ORT): Overview

**License:** Apache-2.0

## Core Capabilities

ORT is described as "a FOSS policy automation and orchestration toolkit" enabling users to manage open source dependencies strategically and safely. The platform generates multiple SBOM formats including CycloneDX and SPDX outputs, along with custom attribution documentation.

## Key Components

The toolkit comprises six integrated tools:

1. **Analyzer** - Maps project dependencies and metadata across various package managers
2. **Scanner** - Detects licensing and copyright data using configurable source code scanners
3. **Advisor** - Gathers security vulnerability information from vulnerability data services
4. **Evaluator** - Applies custom policy rules and license classifications to flag violations
5. **Reporter** - Presents findings through visual reports, notices, and bills-of-materials
6. **Notifier** - Distributes results via email and JIRA tickets

## Policy Compliance

The evaluator component enables "risk-based Policy as Code" for licensing, security, InnerSource, and engineering standards assessments. This allows organizations to automate compliance checking against their specific requirements.

## Accessibility

ORT supports multiple deployment methods: Docker containers with pre-installed dependencies, binary distributions for Linux/Windows/macOS, and native compilation from source code using Java 25+.

# GPL FAQ Brief Summary

**(1) GPL Library in Proprietary Program:**
You cannot incorporate GPL software into a proprietary system. The FAQ states: "The goal of the GPL is that all modified versions must be free software." However, you may distribute them separately as long as they remain well-separated and users understand their distinct statuses.

**(2) AGPLv3 Network Obligation:**
The Affero GPL requires that "modified versions of the software offer all users interacting with it over a computer network an opportunity to receive the source." This applies even when running modified code on web servers.

**(3) GPLv2 and GPLv3 Compatibility:**
These versions are not compatible with each other. Code licensed under "GPLv2 or later" can be relicensed to GPLv3, but pure GPLv2-only code cannot be combined with GPLv3-only code in a single distribution.

**(4) Copying GPL Code Lines:**
The FAQ does not directly address copying small snippets. However, it emphasizes that translation and modification of GPL code constitute derivative works covered by the same license terms, suggesting that even small portions incorporated into proprietary code would trigger GPL obligations.

# SPDX Key Information

**ISO/IEC Standard:** ISO/IEC 5962:2021

**Current Specification Version:** SPDX 3.0.0 (released April 2024)

**Coverage Areas:**

SPDX handles "software bill of material information, including provenance, license, security, and other related information." The 3.0 release specifically introduced "new Security, Build, Dataset and AI profiles" to expand its scope beyond traditional licensing into emerging compliance and transparency needs.

# CycloneDX Specification Summary

**Current Version:** 1.7 (Released 2025-10-21)

**Standardization Status:** CycloneDX is standardized as ECMA-424, published on 2025-12-10 by Ecma International in collaboration with the OWASP Foundation.

**License Information Support:** Yes. The specification includes BOM metadata that covers "license information for the BOM document itself," along with "license and copyright details" for components.

**VEX/Vulnerability Disclosure Support:** Yes. The object model includes a Vulnerabilities section that enables organizations to communicate "known vulnerabilities inherited from the use of third-party and open-source software" as well as "previously unknown vulnerabilities affecting both components and services," making it "ideal for both vulnerability disclosure and VEX use cases."

# Searching the open-source GitHub ecosystem for a specific coding task — tool survey for Daliesk

Date of reading for all prices and docs: **2026-09-04**. "Primary" = vendor page or paper read directly this session; "secondary" = third-party page, flagged where used. Repo licence/star/last-push figures come from the GitHub API (read 2026-09-04 through the GitHub MCP server).

Method note: ~30 web searches plus ~90 direct page fetches; several vendor pages block automated fetching (Sourcegraph docs, Greptile docs, EUR-Lex full text), so a few items are marked unverified in section (d). I also ran live probes of five endpoints (GitHub `search_code`, Firecrawl developer search, HF Hub search, DeepWiki MCP, grep.app MCP, Context7 MCP) to check auth requirements and result formats.

---

## 1. Tool-by-tool

### 1.1 GitHub-native

**GitHub code search (REST `GET /search/code`, UI, MCP)**
- What: lexical search over default branches of public repos (and repos you can read), with `repo:`/`org:`/`language:`/`path:`/`filename:` qualifiers and `text_matches` fragments. Engine is Blackbird: sparse-gram index over "45 million repositories", "15.5 billion documents", "115 TB of code" deduplicated to ~28 TB unique content by sharding on Git blob object ID; per-shard p99 ~100 ms (GitHub engineering post).
- Licence: proprietary service.
- Quality evidence: none published as retrieval benchmarks; it is exact-match ranking, not semantic. Live probe: `"token bucket" rate limiter redis language:go` returned 1,716 files in <1 s (traefik, go-ramjet, ...).
- Pricing/limits (primary, docs.github.com/en/rest/search/search): free; "requires you to authenticate and limits you to 10 requests per minute"; max 1,000 results per query; only files <384 KB; default branch only.
- Reverse-engineer: **content-addressable dedup by blob SHA** — collapse identical files across forks before ranking, and use the blob hash as the cache key for anything you fetch or summarise.

**GitHub Copilot coding agent (cloud agent)**
- What: assign an issue / `@copilot` / MCP `create_pull_request_with_copilot`; the agent researches the repo, plans, edits on a branch, opens a PR. It uses Copilot's per-repository **semantic code-search index** ("initial indexing can take up to 60 seconds for a large repository", "no limit to how many repositories you can index", updates "within seconds"). It "can only make changes in the repository specified when you start a task" — it is not an ecosystem search tool.
- Licence: proprietary.
- Quality evidence: none published for its retrieval component.
- Pricing (primary, docs.github.com plans + usage-based-billing-for-individuals): Pro $10/mo (1,500 AI credits: 1,000 base + 500 flex), Pro+ $39 (7,000), Max $100 (20,000), Business $19/seat (1,900 credits/user/mo), Enterprise $39/seat (3,900). "1 AI credit = $0.01 USD"; the agent "consumes GitHub Actions minutes and AI credits", amount depends on model and tokens. Premium-request units are legacy for cohorts "who remained on legacy premium request-based billing after June 1, 2026" (docs); the switch date is otherwise reported by secondary press (Visual Studio Magazine, 2026-04-27).
- Reverse-engineer: **lazy per-repo semantic index built at first task with sub-minute SLO and incremental refresh** — index a candidate repo only when it enters the top-k, and reuse it across tasks.

**Official GitHub MCP server (`github/github-mcp-server`)**
- What: MIT-licensed Go server (32,706 stars, pushed 2026-09-03) exposing toolsets incl. `search_repositories`, `search_code`, `get_file_contents`, `search_issues`, `search_pull_requests`, `search_commits`; remote endpoint `https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/` with OAuth or PAT; remote GA since 2025-09-04 (GitHub changelog). `search_repositories` with `minimal_output:false` returns full repo objects (my probe returned `license.spdx_id`, `stargazers_count`, `pushed_at`, `archived`, `created_at` for 13 repos in one call). A `fields` parameter trims payloads.
- Licence: MIT (LICENSE: "Copyright (c) 2025 GitHub").
- Quality: inherits GitHub search; no independent eval.
- Pricing: free; REST rate limits apply (code search 10/min; repository search shares the general search bucket).
- Reverse-engineer: **`fields`/`minimal_output` output budgeting per tool** — the same REST call can cost 300 or 5,000 tokens of agent context depending on projection.

**GitHub Spec Kit (`github/spec-kit`)**
- What: MIT toolkit (133,411 stars, pushed 2026-09-03) providing the `specify` CLI and slash commands `/speckit.constitution`, `/speckit.specify`, `/speckit.plan`, `/speckit.tasks`, `/speckit.implement`, `/speckit.clarify`, `/speckit.analyze`, `/speckit.checklist`, `/speckit.converge`, `/speckit.taskstoissues`; "30+ AI coding agents". It performs no external code search.
- Licence: MIT. Pricing: free. Quality evidence: none (not a retrieval tool).
- Reverse-engineer: **derive search queries from structured artifacts** — the spec/plan/tasks triple is the natural place for Daliesk's workflow to mint retrieval queries (per task, per named dependency) rather than from the raw prompt.

### 1.2 Code-intelligence platforms

**Sourcegraph: Code Search, Deep Search, MCP; Cody; Amp**
- What: Code Search over repos you connect (keyword + `nls_search` semantic + SCIP precise navigation); **Deep Search** is an agentic loop over search/navigation plus "small Lua scripts for analysis" in a sandbox with "no network, system, or general filesystem access", consuming subscription credits, admin-limitable ("60 Deep Search per hour"). The **MCP server** (`https://<instance>/.api/mcp`, `/all`, `/deepsearch`) exposes `keyword_search`, `nls_search`, `evaluator`, `go_to_definition`, `find_references`, `commit_search`, `diff_search`, `read_file`, `code_finder`, `deepsearch`. **Cody** is enterprise-only now; **Amp** is Sourcegraph's agent; its **Librarian** subagent (post dated 2025-10-20) "searches remote codebases" — "all public code on GitHub as well as your private GitHub repositories" once a GitHub connection is configured.
- Licence: proprietary since 2024 — `sourcegraph/sourcegraph-public-snapshot` archived 2024-09-30; `cody-public-snapshot` is the last Apache-2.0 commit.
- Quality evidence: no published Deep Search eval found (blog 2025-06-25 has none; docs list sources per answer but no metrics).
- Pricing (primary, sourcegraph.com/pricing via rendered fetch): single "Enterprise" plan "Starting at $16K" annually, includes Code Search, "AI-powered Deep Search", "Full MCP Server, API, and CLI access", credit pooling. Per-user figures ($49 Enterprise Search, $59 Cody Enterprise) appear only on secondary sites and were not on the page I read. Amp (primary, ampcode.com/docs/pricing): no markup on provider API prices for individuals; Megawatt $20/mo (≥$20 usage), Gigawatt $200/mo; enterprise 50% higher with $1,000 minimum; credits expire after 12 months; Amp Free (launched 2025-10-15) has been curtailed in 2026 (secondary).
- Reverse-engineer: **symbol-graph retrieval with a sandboxed evaluator** — precise definitions/references (SCIP-style) plus a tiny scripting layer to aggregate search hits before they hit the model context; and Amp's **Librarian pattern**: delegate ecosystem search to a subagent with its own context window so raw hits never pollute the main agent.

**Greptile**
- What: full-codebase-indexed AI code review (standard and "TREX" reviews). Its earlier index/query API is not visible on today's site; the docs host returned 503/422 to every fetch, so API/MCP status is unverified.
- Licence: proprietary.
- Quality evidence: vendor benchmark (July 2025): 50 real bug-fix PRs from 5 repos, bugs reconstructed from bug-introducing commits, default settings; catch rates Greptile 82%, Bugbot 58%, Copilot 54%, CodeRabbit 44%, Graphite 6%. Independent critique (DeepSource, Feb 2026): "50 PRs across 5 repos is a small dataset"; Augment's re-run on the same repos scored Greptile "45%, not 82%"; "every vendor that has published one wins their own".
- Pricing (primary, greptile.com/pricing): Starter free (1 active developer, 50 credits/mo); Pro $30/seat/mo incl. 50 credits/seat, 1 credit = 1 standard review, 3 = TREX, "$1 per additional credit"; free for MIT/Apache OSS projects; 50% off pre-Series A.
- Reverse-engineer: **eval construction from real bug-fix commits** — Daliesk can build its retrieval eval the same way (trace fix PRs to the files that had to be read), while avoiding the small-n and self-scoring flaws DeepSource documents.

**Octocode MCP (`bgauryy/octocode`)**
- What: MIT (923 stars, pushed 2026-09-04) Rust-engined CLI/MCP with 17 tools (`ghSearchCode`, `ghSearchRepos`, `ghGetFileContent`, `ghViewRepoStructure`, `ghSearchPullRequests`, `ghSearchCommits`, `npmSearch`, `localSearchCode`, `lspGetSemantics`, ...); needs `gh auth` or a PAT; claims "~2.0× fewer characters than plain gh" (self-reported).
- Pricing: free; GitHub rate limits apply.
- Reverse-engineer: **skeletonise/minify code before it enters context** (signatures and structure first, bodies on demand).

**Onyx (`onyx-dot-app/onyx`)**
- What: open-source enterprise search/RAG/agents platform with connectors; the GitHub connector indexes PRs and issues, "Source code files are NOT indexed". Not a code-retrieval engine.
- Licence: MIT core with `ee/` under the Onyx Enterprise License (GitHub reports `NOASSERTION` because of the mixed tree, 31,923 stars, pushed 2026-09-04); a fully MIT `onyx-foss` mirror exists. Cloud Business tier $20/user/mo (secondary).
- Reverse-engineer: **permission-aware connector sync** (document ACL mirroring), relevant if Daliesk later indexes private repos.

### 1.3 Repo-wiki and repo-context services

**Cognition DeepWiki + DeepWiki MCP**
- What: generated wiki per public repo (structure → pages → grounded Q&A); "over 50,000 top public GitHub repositories" pre-indexed, others indexed on first request. MCP at `https://mcp.deepwiki.com/mcp` (SSE deprecated), tools `read_wiki_structure`, `read_wiki_contents`, `ask_question`. Live probe: `tools/list` succeeds with no auth; `ask_question.repoName` accepts "a list of repositories (max 10)". Private repos via a Devin account.
- Licence: proprietary; MCP free, no key.
- Quality evidence: none published.
- Pricing: public MCP free (docs.devin.ai). Devin (primary devin.ai/pricing): Free $0, Pro $20/mo, Max $200/mo, Teams $80/mo + $40/seat; DeepWiki-private inclusion not stated on the page.
- Reverse-engineer: **wiki generation per repo, cached, with multi-repo questions** — one-time structure+page synthesis turns every later "which files matter" query into a cheap lookup.

**Zread (Z.ai / Zhipu)**

## 2. Retrieval-quality evidence (2025–2026) that transfers to this problem

- **SWE-bench (ICLR 2024, still the reference numbers)**: BM25 file recall with 13k/27k/50k-token budgets — all gold files 26.09% / 39.83% / 45.90%; any gold file 34.77% / 51.27% / 58.38%; oracle vs BM25 more than doubles resolve rate (Claude 3 Opus 9.39% vs 3.79%).
- **SWE-bench Multimodal (Oct 2024)**: RAG baselines 5.5% (GPT-4o) / 5.0% (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) vs 12.2% for the best agent; retrieval-only pipelines lose to interactive exploration on JS/visual repos.
- **SWE-Explore (arXiv 2606.07297, June 2026)**: 848 issues, 10 languages, 203 projects; "agentic explorers form a clear tier above classical retrieval"; file-level localisation is largely solved, "line-level coverage and efficient ranking" separate systems.
- **ContextBench (arXiv 2602.05892, 2026)**: 1,136 tasks, 66 repos, 8 languages, human gold contexts; "sophisticated agent scaffolding yields only marginal gains", "LLMs consistently favor recall over precision", large gap between explored and used context.
- **Agent Retrieval Bench (arXiv 2607.24882, July 2026)**: 427 samples/25 repos; "No single retrieval family dominates" — Qwen3-Embedding-4B best MRR, 8B best Recall@20, RepoMap best budgeted yield at 8K tokens; logged agent trajectories missed gold files in 27–35% of samples.
- **CORE-Bench (arXiv 2606.11864, EMNLP 2026)**: 180K queries; "a sharp drop from traditional code search to code retrieval in agentic coding settings"; simple SFT of embedders recovers much of it.
- **CoREB (arXiv 2605.04615, May 2026)**: 11 embedders, 5 rerankers; short keyword queries degrade sharply; no model wins all of text→code, code→text, code→code.
- **CoIR (ACL 2025; CodeSearchNet successor)**: 10 datasets, 8 subtasks, ~2M docs, merged into MTEB. 2025–26 datapoints on MTEB-Code (jina paper Table 2): voyage-code-3 79.84, jina-code-embeddings-1.5B 78.94, 0.5B 78.72, gemini-embedding-001 76.48, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B 74.69; CodeXEmbed-7B reports >20% over Voyage-Code on CoIR. Licences matter here: jina-code-embeddings are CC-BY-NC-4.0 (not usable commercially without a licence), Qwen3-Embedding is Apache-2.0.
- **Beyond Localization (arXiv 2603.29067, March 2026)**: even oracle localisation leaves success "below 50%" — retrieval is necessary, not sufficient.
- Vendor evals: Greptile 82% (n=50) vs 45% independent; Firecrawl 0.63 recall@10 (n=1,179, self-run); exa-code unquantified; Nia unsubstantiated; Sourcegraph none.

Implication for Daliesk: benchmark **line-/symbol-level context yield under a token budget** (SWE-Explore/ContextBench style), not repo-level hit rate; expect hybrid lexical + embedding + agentic exploration, with reranking, to beat any single API.

## (a) Ranked shortlist for "task description → 10 best repos with licence, activity and exact files, < 60 s"

1. **GitHub `search_repositories` + `search_code` + `get_file_contents` (REST or official MCP)** — the only source returning `license.spdx_id`, `pushed_at`, `archived`, stars and file paths with `text_matches` in the same round trip; $0; constraint: 10 code searches/min per token, so pool GitHub App installation tokens and cap at ~3 code searches per task.
2. **grep.app MCP (`searchGitHub`)** — sub-second regex over ~1M repos for call-site queries; free; undocumented limits, so treat as best-effort with a 3 s timeout.
3. **Exa `search` with `category:"github"`, `type:"fast"|"auto"`, `highlights`** — prose-task → repo discovery; ~$0.007–0.017/call; `includeDomains:["github.com"]` as fallback if the category is retired.
4. **Firecrawl developer search** — issues/merged-PR/README/OpenAPI passages that explain *why* a repo is the right one; 2 credits per 10 results; published recall@10 to compare against.
5. **DeepWiki MCP `read_wiki_structure` → `ask_question` (≤10 repos per call)** — converts the top candidates into "read these files"; free; run in parallel with a 20 s budget and degrade to structure-only when un-indexed.
6. **Context7 `resolve-library-id` → `query-docs`** — when the task names a library/version; 1,000 free calls/month, then $10/seat for 5,000.
7. **Octocode `ghViewRepoStructure`/`ghGetFileContent` (self-hosted)** — token-efficient tree and skeleton reads for the finalists; free.
8. **Repomix `pack_remote_repository --compress` / gitingest** — assemble the final digest of the chosen files within a token budget; free.
9. **Perplexity Search API (`search_domain_filter:["github.com"]`, $5/1k) or Tavily (1–2 credits)** — cheap web fallback for niche ecosystems (Zig, Nim, hardware).
10. **Model-native search (Anthropic/OpenAI $10/1k, Gemini $14/1k after 5k free)** — last resort; no licence/activity facets, tokens on top.

Excluded and why: Sourcegraph (indexes *your* connected repos; $16K/yr floor; not a public-ecosystem index), Greptile (review product, API status unverified), Copilot coding agent (single-repo, no search API), Onyx (no source indexing), Spec Kit (upstream of search, not a source), Zread (locked to GLM Coding Plan), Nia (self-serve limits, unverified quality), HF Hub (models/datasets, not code; substring search).

Pipeline sketch that fits 60 s: query rewrite (1 LLM call, ~1 s) → parallel fan-out to 1–4 (≤3 s each) → merge, dedup by repo and by blob SHA → filter/score on `license.spdx_id` allow-list, `archived=false`, `pushed_at` within 18 months, stars as tie-break → top-10 → parallel DeepWiki structure + code-search `text_matches` → LLM file selection/rerank (one call, ~40k tokens in, ~5–10 s) → digest. Typical wall clock 15–30 s; the LLM rerank and DeepWiki are the long poles.

## (c) Licence hygiene for reusing found code in a European commercial product

- **Detect at file level, not repo level.** GitHub's `license` object comes from Licensee matching the `LICENSE` file only and is `null` when unmatched; vendored directories and single files frequently differ. Run ScanCode (Apache-2.0; licence data CC-BY-4.0) on anything copied, and gate with ORT's evaluator (Apache-2.0) policy-as-code. Emit SPDX licence expressions (`GPL-2.0-only`, `Apache-2.0`) — SPDX 3.0 (April 2024; ISO/IEC 5962:2021 for the earlier version) or CycloneDX 1.7 (ECMA-424, Dec 2025).
- **Copyleft rules (FSF GPL FAQ):** GPL code cannot be incorporated into a proprietary program; AGPLv3 additionally requires that users interacting "over a computer network" can obtain source of modified versions; GPLv2-only and GPLv3-only code cannot be combined; modification/translation of GPL code is a derivative work, so snippet copying is not exempt. Practical policy: allow-list MIT/BSD/ISC/Apache-2.0 (mind Apache NOTICE and patent clause; Apache-2.0 is incompatible with GPLv2-only), review-list LGPL/MPL-2.0/EPL/CDDL, deny GPL/AGPL/SSPL/BUSL/Elastic/CC-BY-NC and `null`/`NOASSERTION` (all rights reserved by default). Concrete cases from this survey: Firecrawl's core is AGPL-3.0 (using the hosted API is fine; self-hosting a modified copy is not without compliance), Onyx mixes MIT with an Enterprise License under `ee/`, jina-code-embeddings weights are CC-BY-NC-4.0.
- **Dedup by licence and record provenance.** Deduplicate candidates by blob SHA, then drop any candidate whose effective licence is outside the allow-list *before* it reaches the model; log `(url, commit SHA, path, line range, SPDX id, retrieved_at)` for every snippet that enters context — Daliesk's "model-visible ⟺ logged" invariant already covers the mechanism; extend it to a snippet-level SBOM entry.
- **EU Cyber Resilience Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/2847:** in force 10 Dec 2024; **Article 14 reporting obligations apply from 11 September 2026** (actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents to the ENISA single reporting platform, 24-hour early warning); **main obligations from 11 December 2027**, including Annex I Part II(1) — an SBOM "in a commonly used and machine-readable format covering at the very least the top-level dependencies"; Article 13(5) requires due diligence when integrating third-party components, including FOSS (verify regular security updates, check vulnerability databases, test); Article 24 creates the "open-source software steward" with a lighter regime; non-monetised FOSS is out of scope (Commission CRA open-source page). Chapter IV (notified bodies) applies from 11 June 2026 per the regulation text; see (d) on verification.
- **EU Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853:** software is a "product" (Art. 4(1)); applies to products placed on the market **after 9 December 2026** (Art. 2(1), transposition Art. 22); FOSS "developed or supplied outside the course of a commercial activity" is exempt (Art. 2(2)) — a commercial harness that ships reused code is the liable manufacturer regardless of the snippet's origin.
- Operational consequence: the SBOM you must have for CRA Annex I is the same artefact that answers "which GPL file got in"; build it from the retrieval log, not from a post-hoc scan.
